title: One Antioxidant Could Be Key to Keeping Aging Muscles Strong, Study Finds
excerpt: Astaxanthin, found in salmon and shrimp, rejuvenated aged human muscle stem cells in laboratory studies — but with a notable sex difference that could reshape treatment approaches.
body:
• Researchers found that astaxanthin, a naturally occurring antioxidant, significantly enhanced the regenerative capacity of aged human muscle progenitor cells in laboratory studies.
  • The compound boosted proliferation and myogenic commitment of aged muscle stem cells, with stronger effects in male cells than female — suggesting sex-specific treatment approaches may be needed.
  • The NRF2-SIRT3 signaling axis emerged as a key driver of the antioxidant's effects on muscle cell rejuvenation.
  • While the findings are promising for combating sarcopenia — age-related muscle loss affecting millions of older adults — clinical trials in humans are still needed.

A naturally occurring antioxidant found in salmon, shrimp, and algae could hold the key to keeping aging muscles strong, according to a study published in npj Aging. Researchers demonstrated that astaxanthin — the pigment that gives flamingos and crustaceans their pink color — can rejuvenate aged human muscle stem cells in the laboratory, boosting their ability to proliferate and form new muscle tissue.

Reviving Aging Muscle Stem Cells

As people age, skeletal muscle gradually loses its ability to repair itself. The culprits are satellite cells — muscle-specific stem cells that normally spring into action when muscle tissue is damaged, generating new fibers to replace what's lost. With age, these cells become less responsive, accumulate oxidative damage, and increasingly fail to do their job. The result is sarcopenia, a progressive loss of muscle mass and strength that affects an estimated 10 to 16 percent of older adults worldwide.

"While the findings are promising for combating sarcopenia — age-related muscle loss affecting millions of older adults — clinical trials in humans are still needed."

The research team isolated human muscle progenitor cells (hMPCs) from elderly donors and treated them with astaxanthin in vitro. The antioxidant enhanced both the proliferation and myogenic commitment of these aged cells — meaning they were more likely to develop into functional muscle tissue rather than sitting dormant or converting into fat or scar tissue.

A Sex-Specific Response

One of the study's most striking findings was a pronounced sex difference. Male muscle cells responded more robustly to astaxanthin treatment than female cells. In males, the antioxidant improved mitochondrial function and reduced mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) — the damaging molecules that accumulate with age. Female cells showed more modest improvements.

The researchers traced the difference to mitochondrial biology. In male cells, astaxanthin increased the expression of SIRT3, a mitochondrial protein linked to longevity, in the mitochondria themselves. This effect was not observed in female cells. The finding suggests that estrogen, which helps maintain satellite cell health in younger women, may play a mediating role — and its decline with age could create different vulnerability patterns between sexes.

The NRF2-SIRT3 Pathway

Despite the sex differences, one molecular pathway responded consistently in both male and female cells: the NRF2-SIRT3 axis. NRF2 is a master regulator of antioxidant defense, while SIRT3 governs mitochondrial metabolism and stress response. Both increased with astaxanthin treatment regardless of sex, pointing to this pathway as a fundamental mechanism through which the antioxidant supports muscle regeneration.

Previous research in animal models had hinted at astaxanthin's muscle-protective effects, including reduced fibrosis during disuse and maintenance of capillary networks in unloaded muscles. The new study extends these findings to human cells for the first time and identifies specific molecular drivers.

From Lab Bench to Medicine Cabinet

Astaxanthin is already widely available as a dietary supplement and has a strong safety profile. Small clinical trials have shown it can enhance endurance and muscle strength in elderly individuals undergoing exercise training. But the leap from laboratory cell studies to proven clinical therapy remains significant.

The researchers note that their in vitro model could not account for the complex hormonal environment of a living body, particularly the role of circulating estrogen in women. Future studies combining astaxanthin with hormonal therapy could reveal whether the sex-specific effects persist or can be overcome. For now, the work offers a molecular roadmap for understanding why aging muscles stop healing — and a plausible path to helping them recover.
